For review by the item 26 authors and batch 7b implementers. 2026-09-29;
read against main at `3ec367f4deb8c47d1720da3760240ed0b9f8ce95`.

**Decision supported:** option 1 of [the judgement](comprises-type-level-judgement.md).
Allow coverage to resolve overload overlap without turning coverage into
ordinary subtyping. The original proof can retain runtime uniqueness, but
must give up static uniqueness; the return-type intersection has the short
justification below. This is a conditional, pen-and-paper proof extension,
not a verification of the implementations or full Fortress soundness.

## Source and scope

The source is [Proof of Overloading Resolution for Functions](../../Specification/appendices/overloading-function.tex),
especially `lem:subset`, `lem:le`, `thm:overloading-subtyping` and
`thm:dynamic-subtype-static`. Keep its finite-candidate argument, for
calls applicable **without coercion**. Here declarations have ground domain
and return types; an intermediate argument type such as `G[\ZZ32\]`
is ground too. Assume the existing no-duplicates rule, concrete implementation
availability, body typing, and a sound, transitive subtype relation.
Equivalent domains are identified for ordering purposes.

This does not prove the lift to quantified generic overloads or inference:
their instantiation and Return Type Rule obligations remain with batch 7b.
[Welterweight](../../Papers/Welterweight/evaluation.tick) supplies the useful
notion of a value's *ilk* (its most specific runtime type), but explicitly
says its broader propositions are not rigorously proved. This note does not
claim to finish those propositions.

## 4. The recommendation

Way 2, landing in batch 7b: rung S writes the four passages and the closed-trait case of the Meet Rule; rungs C and W take row 492's repair as a requirement; rung C also types the in-between call.

Why, in order of weight:

1. It is the team's own plan, stated in 2009 and carried in the Working Draft's future-work list: "revise the Meet rule … with the coverage check". The custodians' job (protocol principle 1) is to finish it.
2. It finishes what 7C adopted. Every place both implementations use a clause already reads values: exclusion on both paths, below-a-union and the abstract-method check in the checker; and the checker already finds a coverage meet in the shape its normalizer reaches (measured). The meet is the last place, and the two paths already disagree there.
3. It changes no measured verdict but row 492's two expected failures, no library line and no model line.
4. Way 4 needs the same code plus a rule of ours; way 1 defers the same text to a second rewrite of the same chapter.

# The passages that read `comprises` at the level of types: the judgement

The question. Climb batch 7C rewrote the traits chapter to the type group's 2012 reading of a `comprises` clause: the clause says to which types a trait's values belong, and a trait with static parameters may stand unlisted between a closed trait and its listed types when every trait or object extending it is below a listed type (`Specification/basic/traits.tex:235-252`). Four passages elsewhere still argue from a clause at the level of types: the intersection example (P1, `basic/types-vals-vars.tex:583-604`), the Meet Rule's example (P2, `advanced/overloading.tex:275-307`), the rule on abstract function declarations (P3, `basic/functions.tex:370-415`) and a team draft note (P4, `basic/components/source-code.tex:428-434`). Row 491 asks whether they still hold and what the specification and the two implementations should do. The clean worker's note (`reviews/comprises-type-level-ways.md`, "the ways note" below) lists six ways and marks its own reading. This note checks the deciding claims at their sources, adds one measurement, weighs the ways and recommends one.

## 1. The type question, in plain words

Terms first.

- `trait S comprises { U, V }` closes `S`. The type reading: every type under `S` is under `U` or `V`. This was the Working Draft's note and it is Java's `sealed`. The value reading, "coverage": every value of `S` is a value of `U` or `V`. This is the 2012 Types chapter and Welterweight, and batch 7C's text. A trait has no values of its own; only objects make values. So under the value reading a trait may sit between `S` and its listed types, and it is a type below `S` and below no listed type.
- P1 and P2 conclude "any subtype of both S and T must be a subtype of V. Thus, V = S ∩ T" from the clauses of `S` and `T` and `U excludes W`. That first step needs the type reading. Under the value reading the same steps show that every value of both `S` and `T` is a value of `V`: `V` covers `S ∩ T`.
- P3 and P4 speak of "every immediate subtype" of a closed trait. Under the type reading those are the listed types. Under 7C's text they can differ: `AnyIntegral`'s immediate subtype is `Integral[\I\]`, its listed types the five integer types.

What each source says, checked at its line:

1. The specification's four passages: the type reading (P1 `:583-604`; P2 `:303-307`; P3 `:377-382`, `:413-415`; P4 `:429`). All are 2009 text, Sukyoung Ryu's drafts of 2009-11-02 to 11-06 (`cec470a34`, `a8e403b50`, `0f49d8698`), and the 1.0 release has no such example (ways note section 7; the dates verified with `git log`).

The team's own list of future work, in the same drafts and in the Working Draft: "Identifying the intersection of any two types with comprises clauses with the union of their common subtypes … S&T ~~ V. 4. Welterweight (2012): the value reading in its grammar (`Papers/Welterweight/grammar.tick:21-22`); rule Sub-Comprises, a closed trait is below whatever all its listed types are below (`fig-subtyping.tick:207-211`); the Covered judgement for abstract declarations, "considered to be covered if it is implemented for all the types comprised" (`static.tick:27-47`, `fig-covered.tick`); the Meet rule still asks for a declaration equivalent to the intersection (Meet-Third, `fig-meetrule.tick:56-60`); and its intersection rule, one side below the target or the two sides excluding (`fig-subtyping.tick:48-51`), cannot derive `S ∩ T ≤ V` for the example. So the calculus put coverage into abstract declarations and not into the Meet rule; on the example it is silent.

Guy Steele's last code on it (2012-06-06, `59fdeff62`, its diff opened): a closed trait is below a union when every listed type is, "This should improve the behavior of 'covers' checks in AbstractMethodChecker" (`ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/scala_src/types/TypeAnalyzer.scala:152-157`); the same for trait below trait, commented out, "Gets a stack overflow error; maybe we don't need this in practice. GLS 6/6/12" (`:269-273`).

static type stands between two traits with \KWD{comprises} clauses and their
listed types may have several; the declaration that runs is below every one of
them, and the call's type is the intersection of their return types, which the
Return Type Rule makes sound for declarations without static parameters.
For declarations with static parameters one instance would have to meet every
one of those return types at once, and the type of such a call is not yet
given.
The compiled type checker does not yet enforce across components that every
value of a trait with a \KWD{comprises} clause is a value of one of its listed
types (row~487 of the revival's gap ledger), which the proof assumes.}
subset of $S$ is a supertype of $U$.

A type $U$ \emph{covers} a type $T$ when every value of $T$ is a value of $U$.
A type covers each of its subtypes, and a trait with a \KWD{comprises} clause
is covered by the union of the types listed in the clause
(\secref{trait-decls}).
Covering is a relation between the values of types and not the subtype
relation: a type may cover another type that is not its subtype.

R_D\le R_{\mathrm{call}},

By body typing, a returned value belongs to $R_D$, and therefore to
$R_{\mathrm{call}}$. The proposed call type is sound under the stated
premises and independent of candidate enumeration order. It is the greatest
lower bound of these return contracts, not a claim of globally optimal
inference. This proves neither termination of the called function nor
absence of unrelated runtime errors.


Thus my earlier warning must not be read as a claim that the current checker
keeps coverage wholly outside subtyping. It does not. This is broader than
the measured overload acceptance, although no new assignment verdict was
measured here. It is not, by itself, evidence of an unsafe value conversion.

(and the static-tie justification), reusing clause/exclusion helpers as
appropriate. Do not broaden the shared normalizer merely because the old
one contains a related rule. Preserve existing general subtype verdicts in
this rung; repairing their overall consistency is separate work. The

\note{What is "an intersection of two declarations"?
-- Sukyoung

For function declarations we require that the disambiguating
declaration be the intersection of the pair of overloaded
declarations.}

\paragraph{The Meet Rule for Functions:}
Suppose that $\f(\Ps)$ and $\f(\Qs)$ are two function
declarations in a single scope
such that neither $\Ps$ nor $\Qs$ is a subtype of the other and $\Ps$ and
$\Qs$ are not incompatible with one another.
Let $\mathpzc{S}$ be the set of types that $\Ps$ defines coercions from
and $\mathpzc{T}$ be the set of types that $\Qs$ defines coercions from.
$\f(\Ps)$ and $\f(\Qs)$ are a valid overloading if
there is a declaration $\f(\Ps \inter \Qs)$ in the scope.

all of the following hold:
\begin{itemize}
\item
either $\Ps \excludes \Qs$ or there is a declaration $\f(\Ps \inter
\Qs)$ in the scope,
and
\item
either $\Ps \morespecific \Qs$ or $\Qs \morespecific \Ps$ or for all
$\Ps' \in \mathpzc{S}$ and $\Qs' \in \mathpzc{T}$ one of the two
conditions holds:
\begin{itemize}
\item
$\Ps' \excludes \Qs'$, or
\item
there is a declaration $\f(\Ps' \inter \Qs')$ in the scope.
\end{itemize}
\end{itemize}

Where the Meet Rule for functions asks for a declaration $\f(\Ps \inter \Qs)$ in
the scope, it is also satisfied by declarations in the scope whose parameter
types are each a subtype of both $\Ps$ and $\Qs$ and together cover
$\Ps \inter \Qs$ (\secref{internal-types}): every value of both $\Ps$ and $\Qs$
is a value of the parameter type of one of them, for every value a program can
make, not only for the values a program does make.
Each such declaration is more specific than both $\f(\Ps)$ and $\f(\Qs)$, and
at run time it is applicable to every argument whose value its parameter type
holds.
Every pair of the covering declarations must satisfy the overloading rules in
turn, as every pair of the set must.
This case does not apply to the condition on the types from which $\Ps$ and
$\Qs$ define coercions: covering does not choose between two coercions.

declaration on the intersection itself, and the draft note above asked what the
intersection of two declarations is.

nearest `## ` or `### ` heading above it, its section. Its title is its bold
opening, or where it has none, its opening words up to the first colon,
semicolon or full stop.

A pointer is another entry's number in the sentence that needs it, alone
(`It builds P-48.`) or with the first words of the target's title in quotes
(`It builds P-48, "A type parameter the arguments do not fix ..."`, or
`P-48 ("...")`). Quoted words must open the target's current title (`...` or
`…` marks words left out); when an entry is retitled, the tool rewrites them
in every entry that points to it, in the same call.

The history (FACTS-history.md, POSITIONS-history.md beside the record) holds,
under `### F-87`, one block per change, oldest first: one provenance line (the
UTC time from the clock, the kind of change, `from` each report section,
`commit`, `by`, then the note after a colon), and the line as it stood before
the change. The tool derives the kind: `added`, `rewritten`, `moved to "S"`,
`merged into F-n`, `F-n merged in`, `removed`, `noted`; the numbering wrote one
`numbered` block per entry. A retitle that refreshed other entries' pointer
words, or a merge that moved their pointers, says so in one more line of the
block (`pointer words refreshed in: F-12, P-48`).

A `noted` block, which `note` writes, leaves the entry as it is. It adds what
the entry's history lacks, such as the curator's messages behind a text kept
word for word, with their times, or a correction of an earlier block. It holds
no earlier line, and its note says what it adds, so it needs one. A gone entry
takes none: its last block stays `merged into` or `removed`. A noted block
that corrects an earlier block names it by its time, in the field after the
kind: `correcting the block of 2026-10-13 19:07Z`, or, where blocks of the
entry share that minute, `correcting the 2nd block of 2026-10-14 04:41Z`,
counted oldest first. The block corrected is never edited.

Every write takes a lock (flock on .record.lock beside the record), checks the
state it would leave, appends the history blocks first and then replaces each
record file in one step. A write is refused only for what would break the
store: a bad number, a pointer that does not resolve or whose words do not
open its target's title, a line break in an entry, no provenance (neither
`--from` nor `--note`; for a noted block, no `--note`), a correction that
names no block or more than one, two blocks for one entry in one call.
Never for size. The tool does not commit: commit the record file and its
history together.

  apply FILE                     many changes from one file, all or none (below)
      record.py apply chunk3.md --by 'consolidation chunk 3'
  check [--base COMMIT]          the store's checks; exit 1 on a failure
      record.py check --base cc9424c2a

An apply file holds, in any order: `## TITLE` or `### TITLE`, the section the
new entries below it go to (an existing entry stands under no heading, or
under its own section's, or the `## ` one that holds it); entry lines as they
should stand, `- F-87 ...`, or `- F-?1 ...` for a new entry, its placeholder
replaced by its number everywhere in the file; `move F-87 to SECTION`;
`remove F-90`; `merge F-91 into F-87`; `note F-87`, or `note F-87 correcting
TIME`, a noted block. Each may be followed by one indented provenance line of
its own:
`  from: PATH, "HEADING"; commit: HASH; by: WHO; note: WHY`. Blank lines and
`<!-- -->` comments are ignored. An entry line equal to the entry is skipped:
to add to its history, write `note F-87`. A note whose block the history holds
already, all but its time, is skipped too, so a file run twice writes nothing
twice. One call writes one block per entry, so an entry is noted, or changed,
once in a file.

check fails on: an entry line without its number, or a line under an entry
that continues it; a number on two lines; a number with no `numbered` or
`added` block, or one gone from its file whose last block is not `merged into`
or `removed`; a noted block that holds an earlier line, or whose `correcting`
names no earlier block of its entry, or more than one; a pointer to no live
entry, or quoted words that do not open the target's title; with --base, an
entry at COMMIT that is neither its line now nor the earlier line of a block
in its history (pointer words refreshed by the tool aside). It reports, without failing: the entries over 600 characters, the
entries without a bold title, and the `--from` paths and the report sections
an entry cites (`PATH`, "HEADING") that do not resolve.

The reads are facts-extract.sh's: `F-87`, `F-87+` (with the entries it points
to and that point to it), `history:F-87`, and the title queries, which fall
back to the former titles in the history.

- P-54 **`QQ`'s `ceiling` and `truncate` keep `ZZ`, their declared result type, and raise an error at +∞, −∞ and 0/0.** The specification's paragraph on these methods said that they return the argument itself at those three values (`Specification/basic-lib/numbers.tex`, "Rational Numbers"). That paragraph is revised. `floor`, `round` and the brackets ⌊x⌋ and ⌈x⌉ are built on `ceiling` and `truncate`, so they raise too. Why: the declared integer result wins, and other languages raise there too, as Python's `math.floor(inf)` does. Built: the library raises `DivisionByZero`. Later, a rung after the switch-over makes `QQ` follow the float ruling (P-68): `floor` and `ceiling` then keep `QQ`, and the brackets, `round` and `truncate` give `ZZ`. Still to build: that rung, beside P-68's rung for the float types (PLAN, phase 4, "After the names").
- P-55 **A size may hold arithmetic, compared by its written form once its numerals are computed.** The compiled checker accepts a sum, a difference, a product or a power as a size, such as the length in `Vector[\RR64, 16\]`. It computes the parts written in numerals, so `2 3` is the size `6`. Otherwise it compares two sizes by their written form: `s0 s1` is not the same size as `s1 s0`, though their values are equal. On the compiled path, the class loader computes a size's value when it makes the class of an instantiation. The checker counts a size name, such as `b0`, as possibly equal to a numeral, as the team's Q&A in `Specification/appendices/internal-document.tex` answers. So the `N[\0\]` arm of a `typecase N[\b0\]` is reachable. The library keeps the team's sizes written as products and sums, such as a matrix's storage of `s0 s1` cells. Built (F-146 states what the checker accepts).
- P-56 **The open range `(:)` keeps its wildcard type, and its five cutting methods fail.** `(:)` is the range of every index, as in `a[:]`. It is the object `TrivialOpenRange`, which stays an `OpenRange[\Any\]`: the team used `Any` as a wildcard for any index type. Its methods `truncL`, `truncR`, `every`, `imposeStride` and `atMost` cut a range, so each must answer a range over `Any`. The library's range operators build ranges only over `ZZ32` and its pairs and triples, and a range over `ZZ32` is not a range over `Any`. So no body that answers a range passes the compiled checker. Each of the five is a `fail` with a message, the team's own device for a body that cannot answer its declared type. Nothing in the tree calls them on `(:)` but the five `TrivialOpenRange...Stop` tests that pin the `fail`. The other way, `(:)` as a range over `ZZ32`, is not taken. Why: under walk, a probe found that it made more small programs lose their value than gain one (`reviews/ranges-and-index-types.md`, section 5). Built.
- P-57 **`LexicographicReduction.isLeftZero` takes `TotalComparison`, so the team's answers are reached.** `LexicographicReduction` is the library's reduction behind `BIG LEXICO`, which combines comparisons in dictionary order. `isLeftZero(c)` says whether `c LEXICO x` is `c` for every `x`. The team declared `isLeftZero(_:EqualTo)` as `false` and `isLeftZero(_:Comparison)` as `true`. But the object also inherits `ReductionWithZeroes.isLeftZero` at `TotalComparison`, which answers `false`. That declaration is more specific, so the team's `true` was never reached. The team's overload is now declared over `TotalComparison`, so it replaces the inherited one: `LessThan` and `GreaterThan` answer `true`, and `EqualTo` `false`. Why: the curator wants the compiled checker's error count on the interpreter's library at zero, and this removed the count's last error in an api file (F-53 holds the count). Built.
- P-58 **Every native binding is a `builtinPrimitive` call naming a static helper.** A native binding is a library body that is exactly `builtinPrimitive("…")`, the library's own form, and it keeps that form. Its string names a static Java method in `nativeHelpers/`, the compiled path's helpers, and no longer one of walk's glue classes, which the compiled path cannot use. Walk loads the named helper through a loader beside its glue classes. The compiled path, at the parse and before the checker, rewrites each such body into a synthetic `import java` of the helper and a call to it. It refuses a string that names no helper. PLAN's natives rungs move the bindings onto helpers, and the compiled checker sees each rung's bindings as that rung lands, not all at once at the switch-over. The other form, `import java` declarations written in the library itself, is not taken. Still to build: the natives rungs (PLAN, phase 4, "The natives").
- P-59 **Walk chooses a coercion by the run-time value until the switch-over.** Walk has no static types. So where a coercion is needed, walk chooses it by the value's run-time type, while the specification and the compiled path choose it by the static type. This is accepted as the interpreter's limit, and walk is not changed for it before the switch-over. A callout in the coercion chapter (`Specification/basic/conversions-coercions.tex`) states the limit. Two expected-failure tests record it: `XXXCoercionStaticRungC`, the chapter's own printed example, and `XXXCoercionStaticNarrowRungC`. After the switch-over, walk uses the static coercions that the checker inserts. MicroGPT's static types are concrete, so on microGPT walk's choice and the static choice agree. Still to build: walk's use of those coercions, after walk runs the checker on its programs (P-12; PLAN, phase 4).
- P-60 **The specification reads a `comprises` clause at the level of values.** `trait S comprises { U, V }` says that every value of `S` is a value of `U` or of `V`, so another trait may stand between `S` and its listed types. The specification defines "covers" once: a type covers another when every value of the second is a value of the first. The Meet Rule gains a case for closed traits: declarations that each lie below both overloads and together cover their meet satisfy it. So a call whose argument's static type stands between closed traits and their listed types may have several most specific declarations. The call's type is the intersection of their return types, and the declaration that runs is unique only at run time. Why: the proof addendum (`reviews/comprises-type-level-proof-addendum.md`) shows this sound for ground declarations, whose types hold no type variable (`G[\ZZ32\]` is ground), at calls that need no coercion, with the checker's search for coverage kept inside its overloading check. A generic declaration that needs a run-time instance is outside the proof, and the intersection typing is not extended to it. The specification states that boundary. Built: F-175 (the specification), F-76 (the compiled checker) and F-27 (walk's load check).
- P-62 **The `covariant` keyword is future work, off the path to microGPT.** The keyword, with `contravariant`, is the team's 2012 declaration-site variance: under `trait C[\covariant S\]`, a `C[\Dog\]` is a `C[\Animal\]`, as with Scala's `+S`. No library declaration and no line of microGPT uses it. Gap-ledger row 404 records the hole: the compiled checker accepts variance, but the compiled run dies with `IncompatibleClassChangeError`, and walk refuses the program. The future work is declaration-site variance, carried to run time on both paths. When it lands, a rung tries to bring back the specification's sign-refined number types (P-80, a superseded design) as covariant static parameters. Still to build: row 404's expected-failure tests, one on the compiled path and one under walk, owed in a batch rung; no PLAN line names them yet.
- P-147 **An object defines an inherited abstract method when its bodies of that name at narrower parameter types together cover the abstract method's parameter types.** The bodies cover them when every value of the abstract method's parameter types is a value of the parameter types of one of the bodies. A `comprises` clause counts as the compiled checker reads it: a closed trait is covered by its listed types. A body at the abstract method's own parameter types is the plain case. This is the team's rule of 2012, in Steele's abstract-method check of the compiled checker and in the Covered rule of the Welterweight calculus (`Papers/Welterweight/`). So the team's `Library/Pairs.fss` and `ProjectFortress/tests/FileConversion.fss`, whose objects define an inherited abstract operator once for each type that a `comprises` clause lists, stay valid. Walk applies the same rule at load, and its earlier allowance of any one narrower body goes. The traits chapter's sentence, which admitted no narrower body, is revised in the specification's revision form (P-96). Built (F-145), except that the checker and walk still refuse some valid objects whose methods have static parameters of their own (gap-ledger rows 725 and 728).

import re,subprocess
new=open('explorations/coordinator/consolidation-2026-10-22/evidence/positions/p4/clean.txt').read().strip().split('\n')
old=subprocess.run(['git','show','HEAD:explorations/coordinator/POSITIONS.md'],capture_output=True,text=True).stdout.split('\n')
olds={re.match(r'- (P-\d+) ',l).group(1):l for l in old if re.match(r'- (P-\d+) ',l)}
tot_o=tot_n=0
for l in new:
    k=re.match(r'- (P-\d+) ',l).group(1)
    o=len(olds[k])-2; n=len(l)-2; tot_o+=o; tot_n+=n
    print(k,o,n)
    # sentence lengths
    body=l
    for s in re.split(r'(?<=[.!?])\s+(?=[A-Z`(])',body):
        w=len(s.split())
        if w>25: print('   long',w,':',s[:120])
print('total',tot_o,tot_n)
EOF
